Executive verdict

Keep llama.cpp as PrismLocal’s primary runtime-but repair the integration before treating its current benchmarks as evidence for optimization decisions.

The most consequential findings are not missing accelerator features. They are defects and ambiguities in sampling, streaming, prompt construction, cache state, settings application, memory admission, and performance reporting. Those can corrupt output or make an apparent optimization impossible to interpret. The report separates directly supported source findings from untested race risks, external issue reports, and experiments that require physical devices.

Deliverables

The complete report contains all 33 requested sections, the hypothesis audit, competitor research, comparison matrices, architecture and file mapping, correctness gates, implementation DAG, 25 self-contained mission packets, and the root integrator program.

Evidence boundary: I did not compile Prism’s Android application, run inference on a phone, or execute implementation subagents. No speed, memory, energy, or thermal improvement is claimed as measured. The package’s dependency checks and 11 helper tests passed; those validate the program artifacts, not Prism’s runtime. Competitor research includes selected source, official documentation, releases, and issues-not a complete kernel-level certification of every engine.

Repository baseline

The audit uses the current default branch as retrieved at the start of the investigation:

Repository:       gthgomez/PrismLocal
Default branch:   main
Audited commit:   49ed799a3e633c5192c2c03317d1d50ffdc57c4c

llama.cpp gitlink:
bbeb89d76c41bc250f16e4a6fefcc9b530d6e3f3

The gitlink was checked separately from the version-notes document.

Recent lifecycle work matters: the inspected service already performs native teardown off the main thread, with a bounded main-thread wait. An older claim that teardown is entirely synchronous on the main thread should not be carried forward unchanged.

The findings that change the engineering priority

1. Sampling has a concrete correctness defect

Prism calls llama_sampler_sample(...) and subsequently accepts the sampled token again. In Prism’s pinned llama.cpp API, llama_sampler_sample already samples and accepts. The extra acceptance can advance stateful samplers-including grammar and repetition-related state-twice. This belongs ahead of speculative decoding or kernel tuning.

The roadmap also requires fail-closed behavior when a required grammar cannot initialize, rather than silently continuing unconstrained.

2. Streaming is not yet a lossless contract

The Kotlin bridge can discard data after bounded trySend retries. Separately, UTF-8 is decoded across individual drain chunks without a durable incomplete-sequence buffer, and a normalization layer removes replacement characters. That can hide corruption instead of preventing it. The terminal/drain protocol also needs a regression test for a finished producer with more output pending than one drain retrieves.

The repair is a cancellable, bounded, lossless stream protocol with explicit produced, committed, drained, and final boundaries-not an unbounded queue or a faster polling loop.

3. The reload problem is broader than useVulkan

The useVulkan hypothesis is supported: persistence, reload comparison, and the native configuration path do not form a complete contract. More importantly, settings changes can request a reload while ModelManager’s same-model/hash shortcut returns without reconstructing the runtime. A UI settings change therefore does not establish that the running context changed.

The target needs a complete load key and separate requested, applied, and observed runtime state.

4. Prompt and cache semantics need repair before more aggressive reuse

Kotlin constructs flattened conversation text; native formatting can treat it as a single user message. Native overflow handling removes leading tokens. The cache path also calculates reuse information before operations that can shift or invalidate context. These are risks to instruction preservation and valid KV reuse, not merely inefficient prefill.

The proposed replacement is structured messages → canonical template rendering → exact token budgeting → transactional cache decisions. It preserves upstream primitives, but removes unsupported application-level assumptions about system prefixes, positional shifting, and model architecture.

5. Existing performance labels cannot establish the winning configuration

The reported GPU layer count is derived from the request and a capability check, rather than verified placement. Native ttft_ms measures prompt evaluation rather than submission-to-visible-output latency. Benchmark records retain requested configuration and omit important native measurements; unknown terminal outcomes can also enter success averages.

Consequently, a faster number could reflect changed context, fallback, lost output, or different measurement boundaries. Benchmark integrity is Wave 0 work, not documentation added after optimization.

6. Memory admission is insufficiently architecture-aware

Prism already extracts useful GGUF metadata, but readiness uses a fixed KV-per-context-token estimate. Historical throughput and estimated reclaim can also influence eligibility in ways that do not establish safety under current memory conditions.

The roadmap replaces that with architecture-specific estimates, explicit unknowns, allocation-aware fallback, measured peak-memory calibration, and live re-admission. It does not assume every architecture uses ordinary dense-attention KV or that mapped file size equals resident memory.

What the competitor research changes

PocketPal and llama.rn are valuable integration references, not independent proof of a superior inference kernel. PocketPal’s current source contains explicit context-operation ownership, active-completion tracking, applied context settings, device-rule provenance, and a benchmark ownership flag. llama.rn exposes native device enumeration and other useful runtime plumbing. Prism should adapt those ideas without introducing React Native into its Kotlin application.

Competitor code still needs adversarial review. PocketPal’s memory estimator improves on Prism’s fixed heuristic, but applies the sliding-window limit across all layers. That is not a generally valid estimate for a model mixing full and sliding-window attention. Borrow the metadata-driven approach, not the formula unchanged.

MNN is the leading standalone alternate-runtime experiment-not an approved replacement. Its inspected runtime exposes chunk limits, attention/cache options, mmap-related policies, prefix-cache paths, and backend configuration. Those justify a serious controlled comparison, but its conversion and model-packaging costs must be included.

The first NPU experiment need not introduce a second engine. Current upstream llama.cpp has a documented Snapdragon/Hexagon path. That creates a potentially lower-complexity GGUF-preserving experiment before committing to a separate exported-model runtime. It remains a device-, SDK-, model-, and backend-qualified experiment, not a universal Android NPU recommendation. (GitHub)

Direct code reuse has licensing boundaries. Prism is Apache-2.0; ChatterUI’s inspected license is AGPL-3.0, and its application uses the cui-llama.rn fork. Its ideas are useful, but wholesale copying or assuming stock llama.rn behavior would be inappropriate.

Concrete execution recommendation

The critical path in the package is:

Freeze provenance and evidence contracts
    ↓
Lossless streaming and native lifetime
    ↓
Sampling and grammar correctness
    ↓
Structured prompts and exact budgeting
    ↓
Transactional prefix/cache/context behavior
    ↓
Full load key + requested/applied/observed plan
    ↓
Unified Android safety and corrected baseline
    ↓
Controlled upstream update
    ↓
CPU / Vulkan / OpenCL / load / KV experiments
    ↓
Evidence-keyed planner
    ↓
Bounded auto-tuner
    ↓
Root integration and physical-device confirmation

Benchmark records, model intelligence, and hardware probes can be developed as parallel leaf work. Engine.cpp, JNI, bridge, service, and build wiring have one integration owner. Physical benchmarks are serialized on each device even when research agents work concurrently.

The benchmark architecture separates runtime compute, native real generation, and Android end-to-end chat. It measures prefill, decode, visible TTFT, token gaps, load phases, memory, energy, and sustained thermal behavior independently. A corrected-neutral baseline is retained separately from the historical implementation, so fixing an existing correctness defect does not get mistaken for an optimization regression.

When a second engine earns admission

My proposed default gate is a reproducible, equivalent-quality improvement over optimized llama.cpp, delivering at least one of:

25% higher sustained generation throughput;

30% lower end-to-end TTFT on the declared workload;

20% lower energy per completed equivalent task.

These are engineering acceptance thresholds, not measured results or promised gains. Mandatory correctness and lifecycle gates still apply, with normally no more than a 5% peak-PSS regression unless a specific capability tradeoff is explicitly accepted. Broad promotion requires more than one favorable device/model case.

A unique, important model capability can justify a separate product decision. It must not be presented as a speed victory. Without a retained winner, do not implement the alternate-engine adapter.
